issues.item: Triggers: Visual (Body Parts): Specific body parts associated with the event
issues.explanation: The trigger set is not clinically coherent with the validated trauma type of toxic chemical exposure. 'Specific body parts associated with the event,' 'power imbalance,' and 'being alone with women' are much more characteristic of interpersonal/sexual assault formulations than toxic exposure.

issues.item: Triggers: Power Imbalance: Being in a situation where someone has power over me
issues.explanation: Within the Triggers node, the items point to incompatible trauma meanings: body-part cues, gendered interpersonal cues, and power-over-me situations imply an assaultive perpetrator context rather than an occupational chemical exposure event.

issues.item: Triggers: Female Presence: Being alone with women
issues.explanation: For a 62-year-old male bomb disposal technician whose index trauma is toxic chemical exposure, 'being alone with women' is hard to reconcile as a trauma-related trigger. It implies an interpersonal/sexual-threat context that does not fit the stated trauma type and is not supported by the threat items, which instead reflect generalized physical danger/hypervigilance.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Perpetrator Cues: Anything that reminds me of the person who harmed me
issues.explanation: 'Anything that reminds me of the person who harmed me' is difficult to reconcile with toxic chemical exposure, which typically does not involve an identifiable perpetrator. This item suggests an assault/interpersonal trauma formulation and is inconsistent with the stated trauma type and the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Avoid New Relationships: Starting new friendships or relationships
issues.explanation: Avoiding new relationships is hard to reconcile with a 62-year-old married bomb disposal technician whose indexed trauma is toxic chemical exposure; this strategy fits interpersonal trauma or betrayal formulations more than exposure-related PTSD, and there are no corresponding threat, memory, or appraisal items to support an interpersonal-relationship focus.

issues.item: Avoid Being Alone: Being alone in a room or building
issues.explanation: Avoiding being alone in a room or building does not connect well to the rest of the profile. The threat items describe generalized hypervigilance and escape planning, while the trauma type and other selected triggers do not suggest solitary settings as a specific danger cue. This looks like a maladaptive strategy for a symptom pattern not otherwise represented.

issues.item: Power Imbalance: Being in a situation where someone has power over me
issues.explanation: The trigger 'being in a situation where someone has power over me' is difficult to integrate with toxic chemical exposure and the rest of the selected profile. The other triggers are workplace and loud noises, and the threat items reflect environmental danger monitoring rather than coercion or dominance. This trigger suggests an interpersonal/control-based trauma theme that is unsupported elsewhere.

vignette: Kofi had always taken pride in his work as a bomb disposal technician. He had spent decades honing his skills and saving countless lives. But everything changed on that fateful day when he was exposed to toxic chemicals during a routine operation. The smell of antiseptic and the sounds of the hospital where he was treated still haunted him. As Kofi returned to work, he found himself becoming increasingly anxious in the workplace. He would catch himself scanning his surroundings for signs of danger, searching for escape routes before feeling comfortable anywhere. Loud noises, once a normal part of his job, now made him jump with alarm. His colleagues noticed the change in him and grew concerned. Kofi tried to brush it off, but he couldn't shake the feeling that he was constantly on edge. To cope with these feelings, Kofi started working excessively long hours, using the excuse that he needed to stay focused on his work. In reality, he was trying to avoid being alone with his thoughts. He would often volunteer for extra shifts or take on additional projects, just so he wouldn't have to go home and face the silence of his own company. His wife, Ama, noticed the change in him and tried to talk to him about it, but Kofi just shrugged it off, saying he was fine. As time went on, Kofi's avoidance behaviors only intensified. He started avoiding hospitals and ambulances, even going so far as to take detours to avoid driving past them. The smell of antiseptic would transport him back to that hospital room, and he couldn't bear the memories that came flooding back. His colleagues began to notice his absences from training exercises and team meetings, but Kofi just said he was "taking care of some personal stuff." Despite his efforts to avoid triggers, Kofi found himself constantly on high alert. He would react with alarm when someone touched him unexpectedly, and his eyes would scan the room for potential dangers. His wife started to feel like she was walking on eggshells around him, never knowing what might set him off. Ama tried to be patient, but it was taking a toll on their relationship. Kofi knew he needed help, but he was afraid of facing his demons. He was certain that if he stopped working so much, the memories would come flooding back, and he wouldn't be able to cope. He felt like he was trapped in a never-ending cycle of fear and avoidance, with no escape route in sight. It wasn't until Kofi had a close call on the job, when a loud noise sent him running for cover, that he realized he needed help. His colleagues staged an intervention, telling him they couldn't keep working with someone who was so clearly struggling. Ama sat him down and told him she loved him, but she couldn't watch him destroy himself anymore. Kofi finally broke down, admitting that he had been living in a constant state of fear since the accident. He was afraid of losing his job, his marriage, and even himself. With tears streaming down his face, he asked for help, hoping to find a way out of the cycle of terror that had consumed him.
